title: One Body, One Hope, a New Self
sum: Chapter 4 turns from what God has done (chapters 1 to 3) to how the readers should live. Paul, writing as a prisoner, appeals for unity (4:1-6) and bases it on seven "ones": one body, one Spirit, one hope, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God. Christ then gives gifts to every member, in the manner of a victor handing out spoil (4:7-16, quoting Psalm 68:18), so that the whole body grows up into him.

The second half (4:17-32) is a contrast between the old way of the Gentiles and the "new self," and it ends with plain rules about lying, anger, stealing, speech and forgiveness. The rules are not a list of rules for their own sake. Each is tied to belonging to one body: we are "parts of one another."
readings: Read this way, chapter 4 is a pastor's teaching for a congregation of Gentile converts in a hard city: keep the peace, use your gifts, leave the old life behind, and watch your speech. The sentences are short and the commands are direct.

Read this way, the chapter is about the church as a living body held together by Christ the head. The unity is given (4:3), the gifts build the body (4:12), and every moral rule is a way of protecting the body's life (4:25, 4:30).

views.H: The readers lived in a province where the Artemis cult, magic, civic feasts and trade guilds filled public life. Gentile converts who stopped taking part could lose business and friends. Paul's list of what to give up (4:17-19, 4:25-31) is a list of habits that held that world together. The appeal to unity also speaks to a church that has Jews and Gentiles, slave and free, in one room. The "prisoner" (4:1) may be in Rome (Acts 28), Caesarea (Acts 24) or, some propose, Ephesus.
views.C: Large parts of chapter 4 run parallel to Colossians 3 (4:2-4 with Colossians 3:12-15; 4:22-32 with Colossians 3:5-10). Whether one author used himself twice, or a follower used Colossians, is the main argument about authorship (see the book page). The "gifts" list (4:11) differs from the lists in Romans 12 and 1 Corinthians 12, with no miracles or tongues. The Psalm quotation (4:8) follows no known text exactly. The words "lower parts of the earth" (4:9) and the "full-grown person" (4:13) are the chapter's hardest phrases.
views.L: 4:1 begins the second half of the letter with the key verb "walk" (4:1, 4:17, 5:2, 5:8, 5:15). Verses 4-6 are a compact creed in a pattern of three. Verses 7-16 form a unit: a Psalm quotation in the middle (4:8-10) sits between statements of gift (4:7) and purpose (4:11-16), and the whole ends where it began, with "love" (4:2, 4:16). The contrast with how the readers learned Christ (4:20) and leads to the "old self" and "new self" of 4:22-24, which use clothing language.
views.J: The seven "ones" echo the Shema: "The LORD is our God. The LORD is one" (Deuteronomy 6:4). The Psalm is read in some Jewish tradition of Moses' ascent of Sinai to receive the Torah and give it to Israel, and Paul's change from "took" to "gave" may be tied to that tradition. The criticism of the Gentiles' mind (4:17-19) is a Jewish commonplace, found in Wisdom of Solomon and Romans 1; what is new is that Paul says it to Gentile believers and tells them to stop. "Walk" is the verb behind the later Jewish word halakhah.
views.T: Irenaeus used 4:9 for Christ's descent to the dead (Against Heresies 5.31.1), and the Orthodox icon of Easter shows Christ standing on the broken gates of Hades and raising Adam and Eve. Jerome wrote a commentary and Chrysostom a full set of homilies on Ephesians. Churches read 4:11-12 in different ways: Calvin took only pastors and teachers as ordinary, lasting offices, while Catholic and Orthodox churches see the apostles' office continued in the bishops.

deep.b:
Paul's quotation changes the Psalm in one word, "took" to "gave," and then reads it of Christ. The Psalm is a victory song: God goes up to his mountain, leads captives, and receives tribute. A conqueror who takes spoil also shares it. Paul says Christ has done both. The comment on the quotation (4:9-10) is a puzzle: "he went up" implies a coming down. Three readings of "the lower parts of the earth" are given in the note: the realm of the dead, the earth itself, or the regions lower than the earth. Which one a reader chooses mostly depends on how the Greek genitive "of the earth" is taken ("the lower parts that are the earth," "the lower parts that belong to the earth," or "lower than the earth") and on whether the letter elsewhere speaks of a descent to the dead (it does not). The Septuagint has related phrases for the place of the dead, but not this one: Psalm 62:10 (English 63:9) has "the lowest parts of the earth" (a superlative), and in Ezekiel 32:18 the Greek has a phrase meaning the depth of the earth. The verses behind the Apostles' Creed's "descended into hell" are mainly 1 Peter 3:19 and Psalm 16:10 as Acts 2:27 reads it; Ephesians 4:9 is one of several used.

The other side of the quotation is the Jewish reading. The Aramaic Targum of the Psalms turns the verse into Moses' ascent: it addresses Moses, who ascended to the firmament, captured captives, taught words of Torah and gave gifts to humans. The Syriac Peshitta also reads "give" where the Hebrew has "receive" (Greever, Tyndale Bulletin 2020). The Targum was written down after Ephesians, and whether its tradition was known in Paul's day is debated. If it was, his reading is a Christian answer to it: not Moses but Christ is the one who went up and gave.
deep.refs: Psalm 68:18; Acts 2:27; 1 Peter 3:19; Matthew 12:40; Ephesians 1:20; Colossians 2:15

deep.h: The old self, the new self and the clothes
deep.b: In 4:22-24 Paul uses clothing: take off, put on. Romans 6:6 had said the old self "was crucified with him"; here it is a task. Colossians 3:9-10 and Galatians 3:27 use the same picture, and many scholars think it grew from the habit of baptism: the candidate removed clothes and put on new ones. No first-century text describes the rite, so the link is a guess, though a common one. The picture also has a corporate side: "the old self" can mean the old humanity in Adam, and the "new self" the new humanity in Christ that Ephesians 2:15 calls "one new humanity." Both can be heard at once. The two selves are described by their desires, "deceiving" on one side and "truth" on the other. The rules that follow in 4:25-32 show what the change looks like in a week.

deep.title: "Truthing in love" (4:15) and "speak truth" (4:25)
deep.b: Claude's reading: Paul introduces the idea in 4:15 with the verb aletheuo ("being true," "truthing") as the way the body grows, and then in 4:25 gives its smallest case with a quotation of Zechariah 8:16. On this reading the rule against lying is not a stand-alone moral rule but the first step in the growth of the body he described a few verses earlier, and the quotation is chosen to match the word. Commentators note that the same root appears in both places and commonly link the two verses; the label "the smallest case of the growth in 4:15" is my way of stating how the link works.

echoes: Deuteronomy 6:4; Psalm 68:18; Psalm 4:4; Zechariah 8:16; Isaiah 63:10; Romans 12:3-8; Romans 6:6; 1 Corinthians 12; Colossians 3:5-17; Galatians 3:27; Acts 20:34; Matthew 12:40; 1 Peter 3:19

settings.by: Paul, a prisoner (as the letter presents him)
settings.to: The believers addressed in the letter: most manuscripts say "in Ephesus," and the readers are mostly Gentiles who have come to faith (2:11; 3:1) in a mixed church of Jews and Gentiles, slave and free, rich and poor
settings.when: as the letter presents itself, while Paul is in custody (Rome about AD 62 is the traditional view if Paul wrote it; many scholars who doubt that Paul wrote it date the letter AD 70-100, and then the custody is the letter's picture of him)
settings.why: To call a church made of people who would never have shared a table to keep the unity that Christ made in chapter 2. The appeal rests on the one God and the one Lord, not on shared background. The readers would have heard it as a call to treat the Jew-Gentile peace as real in daily life. Knowing the audience changes the reading: the seven "ones" are not abstract doctrine but the ground for a particular church to stay together.
views: The readers are the church in Ephesus and its region, where Paul worked for about three years (Acts 19:8-10; 20:31).
The words "in Ephesus" are missing from some early manuscripts (see the book page), and the letter has no personal greetings, so it may have gone to a circle of churches in Asia, Ephesus included.

settings.to: The same readers, especially those who lead and those who serve
settings.when: the same letter (see the dating question at 4:1-6)
settings.why: To show that the church's variety is Christ's gift and not grounds for pride or division. Each member has been given a share (4:7), the leaders listed exist to ready everyone for service, and the aim is a body that matures together. It would have mattered in a church where a patron's gifts and a teacher's standing could set people above or below one another, as was common in Greek and Roman society.
views: The apostles, prophets, evangelists, and shepherds and teachers are the church's leadership, whom Christ gave to ready everyone else for service.
The words name people with a gift, not formal offices, and the passage is about the whole body's growth rather than a chain of command.

settings.to: The Gentile believers in the churches addressed
settings.when: the same letter (see the dating question at 4:1-6)
settings.why: To tell converts what to leave behind and what to take on. In a city where religion, trade and civic life were bound together, Gentile believers needed plain instructions: stop lying, stop stealing, watch your anger and your speech, forgive. The "once you were, now you are" pattern would have been familiar to people who had recently been baptized. The section gives teaching on the Christian life in terms of what is natural to the new self, not of rules from outside.
views: The section is Paul's application of his teaching, shaped to the readers' situation.
Some scholars think the section draws on early teaching given to those preparing for baptism, which explains its likeness to Colossians 3 and other letters.

Baptism in water with the Trinitarian formula is the one baptism. It forgives original and personal sin, makes the person a child of God, and cannot be repeated because it leaves a permanent mark (Catechism of the Catholic Church 1213, 1263, 1272).
The Creed confesses "one baptism for the remission of sins." Chrismation, the anointing that gives the "seal of the gift of the Holy Ghost," is given right after baptism.

Baptism is not just water but water combined with God's word and command. It works forgiveness, delivers from death and the devil, and gives eternal salvation to all who believe this (Luther, Small Catechism, on Holy Baptism).
Baptism is "a sign and seal of the covenant of grace," given to believers and to the infants of believing parents (Westminster Confession 28).
Baptism is "a sign of Regeneration or new Birth," and the baptism of young children is to be retained in the church (Thirty-Nine Articles, article 27).
Baptism is the immersion of a believer in water, "an act of obedience symbolizing the believer's faith in a crucified, buried, and risen Saviour" (Baptist Faith and Message 2000, article 7).
Most Friends (Quakers) hold that the true baptism is the Spirit's inward work and do not practice water baptism; some Friends, such as holiness and Evangelical Friends, do.
Christ went down to the realm of the dead to free the righteous who had died before him. The Creed says he "descended into hell" (Catechism 632-635).
The Easter icon shows Christ standing on the broken gates of Hades and pulling Adam and Eve up by their wrists.

The Formula of Concord says the whole person of Christ, God and man, went down to hell after the burial, conquered the devil, destroyed hell's power and took from the devil all his might. It tells readers not to speculate about how (Solid Declaration, article 9).

The Heidelberg Catechism (Q&A 44) reads "descended into hell" of the anguish and torment Christ endured, above all on the cross, which delivers believers from the anguish and torments of hell. Calvin gave this reading (Institutes 2.16.10).
Article 3 of the Thirty-Nine Articles says: "As Christ died for us, and was buried, so also is it to be believed, that he went down into Hell."

traditions.q: Are there still apostles and prophets, and is "shepherds and teachers" one office?
views: The bishops have "taken the place of the apostles as pastors of the Church," and Peter's office as first of the apostles was meant to be passed on to his successors (Catechism 861-862, 1555).
Orthodox theology holds that all legitimate bishops are successors of Peter and that priests are successors of the apostles.

God instituted the ministry of teaching the gospel and giving the sacraments (Augsburg Confession 5). No one should teach publicly in the church or give the sacraments unless he is regularly called (article 14).

Calvin taught that of the offices in Ephesians 4:11 only pastors and teachers are ordinary and lasting. The Lord raised up apostles, prophets and evangelists at the beginning of his kingdom, and sometimes raises them up again when the times need it (Institutes 4.3.4).

Article 23 says it is not lawful for anyone to take on the office of public preaching or of ministering the sacraments in the congregation before he is lawfully called and sent, by men who have public authority given them to call and send ministers.
A local church has two offices, pastor (also called elder or overseer) and deacon (Baptist Faith and Message 2000, article 6). The article limits the pastoral office to men.

The Assemblies of God (General Presbytery statement, 2001) says the gifts of Ephesians 4:11 still exist but that the titles "apostle" and "prophet" need not be used, and it disapproves of formally naming people prophets. Some other movements, such as the Latter Rain movement, taught that apostles are restored; Pentecostal denominations criticized it.

title: Light, the Spirit and the Household
sum: Chapter 5 asks the readers to imitate God, to walk in love as Christ loved, and to live as "children of light" (5:1-14). It then asks them to be wise with their time, to be filled with the Spirit instead of drunk with wine, and to show it in song, thanks and mutual submission (5:15-21). The last half (5:22-33) opens the household instructions, with wives and husbands, and joins them to the picture of Christ and the church.

This is the most debated chapter of the letter. Whether verse 21 sets the rule for what follows, what "head" means, how far "in everything" goes, and what is "great" about the mystery of verse 32 are questions that churches have answered in different ways for centuries. The cards below set the answers side by side.
readings: Read this way, 5:22-33 is a teaching about Christian marriage. The wife submits as to the Lord, the husband loves as Christ loved the church, and the two become the picture of Christ and his people.
A picture of Christ and the church

Read this way, the main subject is Christ's love for the church, shown first (5:25-27) and then used to show what marriage should look like. Paul says so at the end: "I am speaking about Christ and about the church" (5:32).
A reworking of a household code

Read this way, Paul takes a form his readers knew from Greek and Roman writers, in which the head of the house is told how to manage wife, children and slaves, and changes it: he addresses each member directly, gives husbands a duty to love, and sets all of it under the Lord.

views.H: By the time of Julius Caesar, Roman marriage had largely moved away from passing the wife into her husband's legal power: she stayed legally part of her own family. In daily life the husband was still the head of the house. Wives also kept their own property. A Gentile woman who became a believer in a household of an unbelieving husband had much to risk. Public drinking feasts, the cult of Dionysus and the guilds' dinners surrounded the church (5:18). The household code was a known genre (Aristotle, Josephus and others), and some think Christians used it to show they were good neighbors in a society that distrusted new cults.
views.C: Ephesians 5:19-20 parallels Colossians 3:16-17 and 5:22-6:9 parallels Colossians 3:18-4:1; Ephesians is about twice as long, and where it differs it gives more reasons (the Christ and church pattern). The quotation in 5:14 has no known source. In the earliest manuscripts the Greek of 5:22 has no verb (see the variant), and 5:21 is a participle depending on "be filled": the hinge between worship and household. The words "head" and "mystery" are in dispute. The Byzantine text adds "of his flesh and of his bones" to 5:30.
views.L: The chapter is built from three imperatives ("become imitators" 5:1; "walk" 5:2, 5:8, 5:15; "be filled" 5:18) and a chain of participles (5:19-21) that leads straight into the household. Paul quotes a hymn (5:14), Genesis 2:24 (5:31) and uses the analogy of marriage and Christ's love so that each explains the other. The words "holy and without fault" (5:27) recall the letter's first chapter (1:4).
views.J: Imitating God is the old Jewish call to be holy as God is holy. The light and darkness language is also found at Qumran. The bride image runs through Isaiah, Hosea and Ezekiel. The quoted Genesis verse was also read in Jewish writing about marriage, and Jewish tradition honored the Song of Songs as a love poem of God and Israel. Josephus (Against Apion 2.201) shows a Jewish author teaching a wife's submission, and the Talmud (Yevamot 62b) says a man should love his wife as himself and honor her more than himself; Paul's passage has both kinds of statement.
views.T: Chrysostom's twentieth homily on Ephesians is the best-known early sermon on 5:22-33, putting the weight on the husband's love. Augustine said the word added to the water makes the sacrament (on 5:26). The Vulgate's sacramentum in 5:32 was one of the texts Catholic writers cited for marriage as a sacrament, while Luther and Calvin answered that the Latin misled. The 1662 Prayer Book says marriage signifies the mystical union between Christ and his Church. In the twentieth century the passage was at the heart of the debate between complementarian and egalitarian readers.

deep.b: In the Greek, 5:18-21 is one sentence: "be filled with the Spirit," and then five participles: speaking, singing, giving thanks, and "submitting yourselves to one another." The last participle opens the household instructions, and 5:22 has no verb of its own in the earliest manuscripts; it borrows from 5:21. Two readings follow. (1) Mutual submission. "One another" means all believers, and wives, husbands, children, parents, slaves and masters are each shown how to submit and serve (this is the view in egalitarian teaching, and in John Paul II's reading on the Catholic card). (2) Ordered submission. "One another" means "some to others", and the household list says who submits to whom (this is the view in complementarian teaching). Both agree that the husband is told to love with the love Christ showed, and that the reasons given are "in the Lord." A third view, the cultural-form reading in the setting of 5:22-33, holds that the form still comes from the customs of the day. The cards show how churches state it.

Aristotle (Politics 1.1253b) describes the household as three relations: master and slave, husband and wife, parent and child. Writers after him, Stoics and Jews such as Philo and Josephus among them, treated these relations in lists of duties. The New Testament has several: Colossians 3:18-4:1, Ephesians 5:22-6:9, 1 Peter 2:18-3:7, Titus 2:1-10. Differences from the pagan versions are notable. Ephesians addresses the wives, children and slaves themselves, not only the master of the house, and calls them to a Christian reason ("in the Lord"). It tells husbands to love, and sets the pattern in Christ's self-giving. It gives masters a duty and puts them under the same Lord. Yet the code leaves in place the structure of Roman household life, including slavery. That is why readers have taken it both as a radical change from inside and as a baptism of the status quo.

Paul quotes Genesis 2:24 and then says, "This mystery is a great one. And I am speaking about Christ and about the church." "Mystery" is the letter's word for what God kept hidden and now makes known (1:9; 3:3-9). Here it points to a hidden meaning in the creation story: the union of man and woman was always a sign of Christ and his people. The Latin Bible used sacramentum for mysterion, and the verse was one of the texts cited in the Catholic teaching that marriage is a sacrament (Calvin reports the argument in Institutes 4.19.35-36). The Orthodox, who use the Greek word mysterion itself, also count marriage among the church's holy mysteries, though not by way of the Latin. Protestant churches generally keep two sacraments or ordinances and read the verse as a picture, not as the institution of a rite. The disagreement is partly about the Latin word and partly about what a sacrament is, and it should not be reduced to a quarrel over one word.

deep.title: The light that makes things visible (5:13)
deep.b: Claude's reading: Paul says that what light shows up "becomes light." On this reading, the line is not about the shame of exposure but about a person becoming a source of light. In 5:8 the readers themselves "are light in the Lord" after having been darkness, and in 5:11 they are told to "show up" the works of darkness. The sleeping and the dead of 5:14 are called into the light by Christ himself. The same thought may explain why Paul links the chapter's ethics (5:3-12) to the hymn (5:14): conversion is what happens when the light of Christ shines on a person's shameful past and turns it into light. This follows the more positive reading of the verb noted at 5:13, which not all commentators accept.

echoes: Leviticus 19:2; Genesis 8:21; Isaiah 26:19; Isaiah 60:1; Isaiah 54:5; Hosea 2:19; Ezekiel 16:8; Genesis 2:24; Song of Songs 4:7; Proverbs 23:31; Acts 2:13; Colossians 3:5-4:1; 1 Peter 3:1-7; 1 Corinthians 6:16

settings.what: Walk in love, walk as light
settings.to: The Gentile and Jewish believers addressed in the letter, many of whom had come from a world of temple feasts and open sexual license
settings.when: the same letter (see the dating question at 4:1-6)
settings.why: To say what imitating God looks like in a city where such conduct was ordinary: love in place of use, thanks in place of crude talk, truth in place of empty words. The list of sins (5:3-5) is the sort of vice list that Jewish teachers used against pagan life; here it is turned on the church itself. Paul wants the readers to bring the light into the dark and not to retreat from it (5:11), and he ends with a hymn calling the sleeper to wake.
views: Do not join in (5:7, 5:11) means keep away from the practices and the people who live this way.
The same verses call the church to show up the darkness by its life, so that those in it are lit (5:13-14).

settings.what: Wise, filled with the Spirit, thankful
settings.to: The gathered church that hears the letter read
settings.when: the same letter (see the dating question at 4:1-6)
settings.why: To describe the life of a worshiping community: wise use of time because the days are evil, the Spirit instead of wine, song to one another and to the Lord, thanks always, and mutual submission. The readers lived with public drinking parties, and the call to be filled with the Spirit gave them another way to be "carried away." The last participle prepares the household instructions.
views: The singing, speaking and thanks describe the church at its meetings.
The list describes the whole of Christian life, not only the assembly.

settings.to: The wives and husbands of the house churches, who heard the letter read aloud in the assembly (the readers were Jews and Gentiles; many wives married to unbelievers)
settings.when: the same letter (see the dating question at 4:1-6)
settings.why: To show married believers how they should treat one another "in the Lord" in a society in which the husband held legal authority. Wives are told to submit as to the Lord; husbands are told to love as Christ loved the church, giving himself up. Unlike household manuals of the time, the passage speaks directly to the wives and gives the husband the harder command. Knowing this changes the reading: it is not a set of rules for outsiders but a charge to those who heard it. Its meaning for churches today is disputed.
views: 5:21 is the rule and 5:22-33 describe how husbands and wives each give themselves, the wife in respect and the husband in self-giving love.
The husband is the head of his wife as Christ is head of the church, and the wife is to submit to him, while the husband must love as Christ did.
Paul works within the household customs of his day and moves them toward Christ's pattern; the form is not a permanent law of the family.

traditions.q: Is being "filled with the Spirit" a second experience or a continuing command?
views: Many Pentecostal churches teach that the baptism in the Holy Spirit is a distinct experience after conversion, shown at first by speaking in tongues. They read Ephesians 5:18 as a call to go on being filled.

Confirmation is the special outpouring of the Holy Spirit, as at Pentecost, and it strengthens the grace of baptism. The "seal" is the sign that God has marked the believer as his own (Catechism 1302-1303).
The Spirit is given at chrismation, the anointing right after baptism, with the words "the seal of the gift of the Holy Ghost."
The Holy Spirit "seals the believer unto the day of final redemption" (Baptist Faith and Message 2000, article 2).

traditions.q: Is it wrong to drink alcohol?
views: Drunkenness is a sin against temperance. The Catechism speaks of avoiding the abuse of alcohol, not of drinking itself (Catechism 2290).
Wikipedia lists the Eastern Orthodox among those who hold moderation, and says the Orthodox fasting rules forbid wine, and by extension all alcoholic drinks, on most fast days.
Wikipedia lists Lutherans among those who accept moderation, and says the Lutheran Formula of Concord (1576) mentions and assumes the use of wine.
The Westminster Larger Catechism (Q. 136) lists "immoderate use of meat, drink, labor, and recreations" among the sins forbidden by the sixth commandment.

Wikipedia reports that John Wesley's General Rules told Methodists against buying, selling or drinking 'spirituous liquors' except in extreme necessity, and that American Methodists later returned to that rule. It gives no current United Methodist position.
The Southern Baptist Convention's 2006 resolution on alcohol expresses "total opposition to the manufacturing, advertising, distributing, and consuming of alcoholic beverages."
The Seventh-day Adventist Church discourages its members from consuming alcoholic beverages.

traditions.q: Should worship music be sung without instruments?
views: Churches of Christ sing without instruments, because the New Testament commands singing (Ephesians 5:19; Colossians 3:16); they point to the New Testament's lack of any authorization for instruments in worship assemblies.

Gregorian chant is to be given "pride of place" in liturgical services, the pipe organ is to be highly valued, and other instruments may be admitted if they are suitable (Sacrosanctum Concilium 116, 120).

The Orthodox Church in America says the tradition of the Orthodox Church is to have no instruments in worship, and that in Christian worship the human voice becomes the chief musical instrument. Organs appear mainly in some Greek and Antiochian parishes in the United States.
The Reformed Presbyterian churches (for example the Reformed Presbyterian Church of North America) insist on exclusive a cappella psalmody.

traditions.q: Does the husband lead the wife, or do they submit to one another?
views: John Paul II wrote that the "mutual subjection" of 5:21 shapes how 5:22 is read, and that the husband is called to love as Christ gave himself (Mulieris Dignitatem 24, 1988). Pius XI's Casti Connubii (1930) had spoken of the husband's primacy and the wife's willing obedience, joined to his love.

Chrysostom's twentieth homily on Ephesians says "the husband occupies the place of the head, and the wife the place of the body," and tells wives to submit. It puts the most weight on the husband, who must love as Christ loved the church, "even if it shall be needful for you to give your life for her."

Luther's Small Catechism, in its Table of Duties, gives 1 Peter 3:7 and a verse from Colossians 3 (on not being harsh with wives) to husbands, and Ephesians 5:22 with 1 Peter 3:6 to wives. It does not quote Ephesians 5:25 for husbands.
The Westminster Confession (24.2) says marriage was ordained for "the mutual help of husband and wife." That section does not state headship.
The 1662 Book of Common Prayer has the wife promise to "obey him, and serve him," and its opening address says marriage signifies "the mystical union that is betwixt Christ and his Church."

The Baptist Faith and Message (2000, article 18) says the husband is to love his wife as Christ loved the church and to lead his family, and the wife is to submit graciously to his servant leadership.

Complementarians: the Danvers Statement (1987) affirms "male headship in the family and in the covenant community," speaks of "the loving, humble leadership of redeemed husbands," and urges wives toward "willing, joyful submission," while holding men and women equal in value. Egalitarians: the statement "Men, Women, and Biblical Equality" says the husband's function as "head" is "to be understood as self-giving love and service" within a relationship of mutual submission (Ephesians 5:21-33).

Marriage is one of the seven sacraments. The Council of Trent (session 24, canon 1) condemned anyone who denies it, and the Catechism (1601, 1617) says marriage between baptized persons is a true sacrament.
Marriage is one of the church's holy mysteries; its rite is called the Mystery of Crowning.

Luther argued in The Babylonian Captivity (1520) that the Latin sacramentum misled: Paul speaks of Christ and the church, and marriage, which exists among unbelievers too, is not a sacrament of the new law.

The Westminster Confession (27.4) names only two sacraments, baptism and the Lord's Supper. Calvin said the Latin translator used sacramentum for Paul's mysterion and that marriage is not a sacrament (Institutes 4.19.34-37).

Article 25 lists matrimony among five rites "commonly called Sacraments" that "are not to be counted for Sacraments of the Gospel." The Prayer Book says marriage signifies the mystical union between Christ and his Church.
Baptists keep two ordinances, baptism and the Lord's Supper. Marriage is God's gift "to reveal the union between Christ and His church" (Baptist Faith and Message 2000, article 18).

title: Children, Slaves and the Armor of God
sum: Chapter 6 finishes the household instructions with children and parents (6:1-4) and slaves and masters (6:5-9). Each group is spoken to directly, and each is told that the Lord stands over the relationship. Then the letter changes its tone. The last long paragraph (6:10-20) is a call to stand against "the schemes of the devil" in God's own armor, because the struggle is not against "blood and flesh" but against rulers, authorities and spiritual forces. It ends with prayer, and with Paul asking for prayer for himself, "an ambassador in a chain."

The letter closes quickly: Tychicus will bring news and encouragement (6:21-22), and a blessing of peace, love, faith and grace follows (6:23-24). There are no personal greetings. This is one of the features that has led scholars to ask who the first readers were.
readings: Read this way, 6:1-9 gives the duties of children, parents, slaves and masters in a Roman household, joined to the Lord's rule over each of them. The passage assumes slavery and tells slaves and masters how to live within it.
The reversal of a household code

Read this way, the passage uses the form of the code to change it: each person is addressed, each answers to a Lord, masters have no advantage with him, and Christ is the model. Slaves are treated as servants of Christ, which gives them a standing the world did not.

For the armor passage, one reading takes the powers as personal spiritual beings who stand behind human evil. Another reading takes them as the forces of institutions and cultures. Both agree that the church's weapons are truth, righteousness, peace, faith, salvation, the word and prayer, not swords.

views.H: A household in a city like Ephesus included the family and its slaves, whose share of a city's population is debated. Roman law gave the father broad power over his children. Ephesus was famous for magic and for its temple of Artemis (Acts 19). The armor was Roman, and Paul lived beside a guard (Acts 28:16). Tychicus was from Asia (Acts 20:4) and was the likely bearer of the letter and of Colossians.
views.C: 6:21-22 repeats Colossians 4:7-8 almost word for word, and the same is true of much of 6:1-9 and Colossians 3:20-4:1. Views differ on whether this shows one author or a later imitator. The armor passage draws on Isaiah 11 and 59 and Wisdom of Solomon 5. The missing greetings, against the personal names at the end of Colossians, are one reason many scholars see a circular letter. In 6:24 the Greek "in incorruption" is hard, and some manuscripts add "Amen" and a note about Rome.
views.L: The armor section is a single image built with participles (girded, put on, fitted with shoes, taken up) around the main command "stand," which appears four times. The list of pieces is not exact: Paul takes the belt from Isaiah 11:5 and the breastplate and helmet from Isaiah 59:17, adds the shoes and the shield, and ends with the sword (compare Isaiah 11:4 and 49:2) and with prayer. The letter ends the way many of Paul's letters do, with a blessing, but without his usual greetings.
views.J: The honor commandment (6:2-3) is from the Ten Words and the Mishnah counts it among the commands with a reward. The armor passage depends on Isaiah's picture of the LORD as a warrior (Isaiah 59:17) and the Messiah's belt (Isaiah 11:5). The idea of angelic powers over the nations (Daniel 10; Deuteronomy 32:8 in the Greek) is part of Jewish thought, as are the angelic armies of the Dead Sea scrolls. Torah law gave Israelite slaves limits and release (Exodus 21:2; Leviticus 25:39-43) while allowing foreigners to be held for life (Leviticus 25:44-46); Paul cites neither.
views.T: Chrysostom's homilies on 6:1-9 urge masters to treat slaves gently, as fellow servants of the same Lord. In the American South, defenders of slavery appealed to the apostles' instructions to slaves and masters (Thornwell's 1861 church address does). The Pentecostal and charismatic movements have built a doctrine of spiritual warfare on 6:12.

deep.b:
Ephesians tells slaves to obey and masters to treat them in the same way, and it does not say that slavery is wrong. In the United States, defenders of slavery appealed to the apostles' instructions to slaves and masters; Thornwell's 1861 church address is one example. The verses also say that slaves and masters stand equal before God ("their Lord and yours", 6:9; "no favoritism"). Historians of ancient slavery note that Roman slavery was not racial, that many enslaved people were freed, and that cruelty was common; few ancient writers called for abolishing the institution.

The text itself does three things that stood out. It addresses slaves directly, as members of the church. It says their true Master is Christ (6:6) and that they will be repaid by him. And it tells masters to stop threatening, since they have the same Lord and he shows no favoritism (6:9). Whether these steps point toward the end of slavery (as Galatians 3:28 and Philemon 16 may) or only soften it is what the churches disagree about; the card sets out how each tradition has answered. Readers should not pass over the fact that the letter's words were used by slaveholders.

The card gives a sample of traditions, not a full list. The Lutheran, Anabaptist and Black church traditions, among others, each have their own long record on slavery, and readers should look to them as well.
deep.refs: Colossians 3:22; Philemon 1:16; 1 Corinthians 7:21; Galatians 3:28; Exodus 21:2; Leviticus 25:39

deep.h: The powers: personal beings or structures?
deep.b:
"Rulers" and "authorities" are in 1:21, 3:10 and here; "world-rulers" occurs nowhere else in the New Testament; and the phrase "spiritual forces of wickedness" in the heavenly world completes the list. Four readings. (1) Personal evil beings, fallen angels and demons under the devil (the long-standing view of the church; the Dead Sea scrolls and 1 Enoch lie behind it). (2) The structures of human life, the spirit of the state, the economy and culture. (3) A mixture: spiritual beings who work through human institutions. (4) A mythic way of describing evil that modern readers should translate.

Whichever is taken, the letter's aim is plain. The powers have been put under Christ (1:20-22), the church is the place where they learn God's wisdom (3:10), and the church's weapons are not the powers' own. Ephesians never tells believers to attack the powers; the word that governs the passage is "stand."
deep.refs: Ephesians 1:20; Ephesians 3:10; Daniel 10:13; Deuteronomy 32:8; Colossians 2:15; Acts 19:19

deep.title: The armor and the guard
deep.b: Claude's reading: Paul wrote while chained to a Roman soldier (Acts 28:16, 20), so the soldier's gear was in front of him every day. The picture of the church in armor may owe something to that. The armor pieces are not Roman copies, though: Paul fills them with Isaiah's God-the-warrior (Isaiah 59:17; Isaiah 11:5) and with his own terms (truth, righteousness, the good news of peace, faith, salvation, the word). I propose that the passage works on two levels: the visible Roman who guards him, and the unseen powers who guard the world's order. Paul uses what he sees to teach what he does not. Commentators note that his armor image has Roman features and Israelite sources; the point about the guard is my own inference from his imprisonment, and it cannot be proved.

echoes: Exodus 20:12; Deuteronomy 5:16; Deuteronomy 10:17; Isaiah 11:4; Isaiah 11:5; Isaiah 52:7; Isaiah 59:17; Daniel 10:13; Wisdom of Solomon 5:17-20; Colossians 3:20-4:1; Colossians 4:7-8; 1 Thessalonians 5:8; Romans 13:12; Acts 19:19; Acts 20:4; Acts 28:16; Philemon 1:16

settings.to: The children and fathers (parents) of the house churches, who heard the letter read in the assembly
settings.when: the same letter (see the dating question at 4:1-6)
settings.why: To speak to children as members of the church and to tell them to obey their parents because it is right in the Lord, with the promise of the fifth of the Ten Words. To fathers, who held great legal power in a Roman household, it says: do not provoke your children to anger, but raise them in the Lord's discipline and warning. The command to children would have been familiar to Jewish and Roman readers alike; the command to fathers was a limit on the father's power.
views: The passage repeats the common ethics of Jewish and Greek households with Christian reasons.
The passage sets limits on a father's power, and treats the child as a person in the Lord.

settings.to: The enslaved and the slaveholding members of the house churches, who, on the letter's own picture, heard it read in the assembly
settings.when: the same letter (see the dating question at 4:1-6)
settings.why: To tell slaves to serve their human masters wholeheartedly as service to Christ, and masters to treat their slaves in the same way, giving up threats, because both have one Lord who shows no favoritism. In a society in which slaves had no recognized standing, to address them as responsible servants of Christ and to put the master under the same Lord was striking. The passage does not call for freeing anyone, and how it should be read has been fought over; see the deep dive and the card.
views: Paul works within slavery and undermines it by the equality of slave and master before the Lord.
The passage accepts the institution as part of the social order of its day and regulates it.
A word to the first readers
The passage was not meant to give a general ruling on slavery as such, but to guide slaves and masters in a particular church.

settings.to: The whole church, addressed as "you" in the plural
settings.when: the closing section of the same letter
settings.why: To end the letter by showing the church how to stand in a world where evil is organized: put on God's own armor, hold your ground, and pray for all the saints and for the apostle in chains. The readers had grown up among magic and fear of powers; they are told that the powers are real, but that Christ is above them (1:20-22) and that the weapons are truth, righteousness, peace, faith, salvation, God's spoken word and prayer. The passage was for a church, not for a lone fighter.
views: The powers are evil spiritual beings under the devil, and the church's task is to stand against them.
The powers are the forces behind human institutions that enslave and deceive.

settings.to: The churches addressed, and Tychicus as the bearer
settings.when: as the letter presents itself, sent from Paul's custody (see the dating question at 4:1-6)
settings.why: To say who is carrying the letter and why: Tychicus will report on Paul and encourage the readers. In the ancient letter, the bearer often added what was too long or too private to write. The blessing is for all who love the Lord, which includes believers outside the first readers.
views: The Tychicus verses show that Paul knew the readers and wanted to send news to them.
The words, drawn from Colossians 4:7-8 and without personal greetings, suit a letter for many churches or a later writer imitating Paul.

traditions.q: What did the Bible's slavery passages mean for the church's view of slavery?
views: The church now teaches that slavery is an offense against human dignity (Second Vatican Council, Gaudium et Spes 27; Catechism 2414). Gregory XVI in 1839 reproved the slave trade as "absolutely unworthy of the Christian name" (In supremo apostolatus).

Chrysostom's Homily 22 on Ephesians tells masters not to threaten or oppress their slaves and to remember that "both their Master and yours is in Heaven." He calls slavery "the fruit of covetousness" but does not call for ending it.
American Methodists adopted rules in 1784 requiring members to free their slaves. Strong opposition led to the rules being suspended in 1785.
William Wilberforce, an evangelical Anglican, led the parliamentary campaign that ended in the Slave Trade Act of 1807.

The Southern Baptist Convention's 1995 resolution on racial reconciliation names "the role that slavery played in the formation of the Southern Baptist Convention," says many forebears "defended the right to own slaves," and states "we lament and repudiate historic acts of evil such as slavery."

The Covenanter (Reformed Presbyterian) presbytery ruled in 1800 that slaveholders could not take communion in its churches. James Henley Thornwell, a Southern Presbyterian, argued in an 1861 church address that Scripture does not condemn slavery as a sin, since Moses regulated it and the apostles gave duties to both slaves and masters.
John Woolman (1720-1772) wrote against keeping slaves, and in 1776 Philadelphia Yearly Meeting made slaveholding a disownable offense (no one was disowned for it until 1778).

traditions.q: Are the 'rulers and authorities' (6:12) personal beings, and how should Christians fight them?
views: The devil and the other demons 'were indeed created naturally good by God, but they became evil by their own doing' (Catechism 391).

Luther's Large Catechism does not comment on this verse, but on the last petition of the Lord's Prayer it says the devil is the believers' 'chief enemy,' who hinders everything they pray for. The weapon is prayer.

Calvin cites Ephesians 6:12 in the Institutes (1.14.13): what Scripture says about devils is meant to keep us on guard against an enemy 'the most daring, the most powerful, the most crafty,' and to make us put on the armor Paul describes.

C. Peter Wagner's 'strategic-level spiritual warfare' treats the powers as territorial spirits to be fought by prayer teams. Critics such as Robert Guelich answer that Paul 'nowhere' gives techniques for battling demons; the usual reading is that believers stand firm in faith, not that they attack spirits.

The Mennonite Confession of Faith (1995, article 2) says Christ, by his death and resurrection, conquered death and disarmed 'the powers of sin and evil,' and that in his suffering he 'loved his enemies and did not resist them with violence.' It does not say whether the powers are personal.
